Title: The Pop-stack-sorting Operator on Tamari Lattices
Authors: Letong Hong
Date: Tue Jan 25 01:07:57 2022

Motivated by the pop-stack-sorting map on the symmetric groups, Defant defined an operator $\mathsf{Pop}_M : M \to M$ for each complete meet-semilattice $M$ by $$\mathsf{Pop}_M(x)=\bigwedge(\{y\in M: y\lessdot x\}\cup \{x\}).$$ This paper concerns the dynamics of $\mathsf{Pop}_{\mathrm{Tam}_n}$, where $\mathrm{Tam}_n$ is the $n$-th Tamari lattice. We say an element $x\in \mathrm{Tam}_n$ is $t$-$\mathsf{Pop}$-sortable if $\mathsf{Pop}_M^t (x)$ is the minimal element and we let $h_t(n)$ denote the number of $t$-$\mathsf{Pop}$-sortable elements in $\mathrm{Tam}_n$. We find an explicit formula for the generating function $\sum_{n\ge 1}h_t(n)z^n$ and verify Defant's conjecture that it is rational. We furthermore prove that the size of the image of $\mathsf{Pop}_{\mathrm{Tam}_n}$ is the Motzkin number $M_n$, settling a conjecture of Defant and Williams.--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Title: Largest-loop-first loop-erased random walk on $\mathbb{Z}^{4}$
Authors: Daisuke Shiraishi, Satomi Watanabe
Date: Thu Apr  2 08:09:25 2026

Let $S = (S(n))$ be a simple random walk on $\mathbb{Z}^{d}$ started at the origin. We study a loop-erasing procedure of $S[0,n]$ that differs from Lawler's chronological loop-erasure. Specifically, we remove loops from $S[0,n]$ in decreasing order of their lengths. The resulting random simple path is called the largest-loop-first (LLF) LERW. For $d=4$, we prove that the expected length of LLF LERW is of the order $n (\log n)^{-1/2 + o(1)}$. In particular, this suggests that chronological LERW and LLF LERW belong to different universality classes. Furthermore, we also prove the convergence of LLF LERW to Brownian motion in four dimensions.--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Authors: Gregory F. Lawler, Xin Sun, Wei Wu
Date: Tue Aug  9 21:32:35 2016

The loop-erased random walk (LERW) in $\mathbb{Z}^4$ is the process obtained by erasing loops chronologically for simple random walk. We prove that the escape probability of the LERW renormalized by $(\log n)^{\frac{1}{3}}$ converges almost surely and in $L^{p}$ for all $p>0$. Along the way, we extend previous results by the first author building on slowly recurrent sets. We provide two applications for the escape probability. We construct the two-sided LERW, and we construct a $\pm 1$ spin model coupled with the wired spanning forests on $\mathbb{Z}^4$ with the bi-Laplacian Gaussian field on $\mathbb{R}^{4}$ as its scaling limit.--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Title: Stack-Sorting Preimages of Permutation Classes
Authors: Colin Defant
Date: Mon Sep 10 03:48:18 2018

We extend and generalize many of the enumerative results concerning West's stack-sorting map $s$. First, we prove a useful theorem that allows one to efficiently compute $|s^{-1}(\pi)|$ for any permutation $\pi$, answering a question of Bousquet-M\'elou. We then enumerate permutations in various sets of the form $s^{-1}(\text{Av}(\tau^{(1)},\ldots,\tau^{(r)}))$, where $\text{Av}(\tau^{(1)},\ldots,\tau^{(r)})$ is the set of permutations avoiding the patterns $\tau^{(1)},\ldots,\tau^{(r)}$. These preimage sets often turn out to be permutation classes themselves, so the current paper represents a new approach, based on the theory of valid hook configurations, for solving classical enumerative problems. In one case, we solve a problem previously posed by Bruner. We are often able to refine our counts by enumerating these permutations according to their number of descents or peaks. Our investigation not only provides several new combinatorial interpretations and identities involving known sequences, but also paves the way for several new enumerative problems.--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

## 1. Introduction

Building on Knuth's stack-sorting algorithm [15], West's ground-breaking work on the stack-sorting map on symmetric groups [23] inspired subsequent studies, including the reverse-stack-sorting map [12] and the pop-stack-sorting map [3]. Recently, there has been considerable attention by combinatorialists on the pop-stack-sorting map [1], [2], [7], [13], [19]. For each complete meet-semilattice M, Defant defined an operator ${\mathsf{Pop}}_{M}$ that agrees with the pop-stack-sorting map when M is the weak order on ${S}_{n}$ [8]. It is defined so that ${\mathsf{Pop}}_{M}$ sends an element to the meet of itself and all elements that it covers. By definition, M's minimal element $\stackrel{ˆ}{0}$ stays the same when ${\mathsf{Pop}}_{M}$ is applied. We say an element x is t-$\mathsf{Pop}$-sortable if ${\mathsf{Pop}}_{M}^{t}(x)=\stackrel{ˆ}{0}$.

Pudwell and Smith [19] enumerated the number of 2-$\mathsf{Pop}$-sortable elements in ${S}_{n}$ under the weak order. Claesson and Guðmundsson [7] proved that for each fixed nonnegative integer t, the generating function that counts t-$\mathsf{Pop}$-sortable elements in ${S}_{n}$ is rational. Defant [9] established the analogous rationality result for the generating functions of t-$\mathsf{Pop}$-sortable elements of type B and type $\tilde{A}$ weak orders.

Introduced in 1962, the n-th Tamari lattice ${\mathrm{Tam}}_{n}$ consists of semilength-n Dyck paths (lattice paths from $(0,0)$ to $(n,n)$ above the diagonal $y=x$) [22]; its partial order will be defined in Section 2. There are generalizations of the definition, most notably the m-Tamari lattices by Bergeron and Préville-Ratelle [4] and the ν-Tamari lattices introduced by Préville-Ratelle and Viennot [18]. Fundamental in algebraic combinatorics [16], the n-th Tamari lattice ${\mathrm{Tam}}_{n}$ is also isomorphic to ${\mathrm{Av}}_{n}(312)$, the lattice of 312-pattern-avoiding permutations under the weak order of ${S}_{n}$ [5].

In this paper, we study the $\mathsf{Pop}$ operator on Tamari lattices. Let ${h}_{t}(n)$ be the number of t-$\mathsf{Pop}$-sortable elements in ${\mathrm{Tam}}_{n}$. A part of a conjecture by Defant [8] is that for every fixed t, the generating function ${\sum }_{n\ge 1}{h}_{t}(n){z}^{n}$ is rational. We confirm this statement by giving the exact formula of the generating function:

Theorem 1.1

Let ${h}_{t}(n)$ denote the number of t-$\mathsf{Pop}$-sortable Dyck paths in the n-th Tamari lattice ${\mathrm{Tam}}_{n}$. Then$\sum _{n\ge 1}{h}_{t}(n){z}^{n}=\frac{z}{1-2z-{\sum }_{j=2}^{t}{C}_{j-1}{z}^{j}},$ where ${C}_{j}=\frac{1}{j+1}\left(\begin{array}{c}2j\\ j\end{array}\right)$ is the j-th Catalan number.

Moreover, settling a conjecture in Defant and Williams's paper (Conjecture 11.2 (2) in [11]), we have the following theorem:

Theorem 1.2

Define $\mathsf{Pop}(L;q)={\sum }_{b\in {\mathsf{Pop}}_{L}(L)}{q}^{|{\mathcal{U}}_{L}(b)|}$, where ${\mathcal{U}}_{L}(b)$ is the set of elements of L that cover b. Then we have$\mathsf{Pop}({\mathrm{Tam}}_{n+1};q)=\sum _{k=0}^{n}\frac{1}{k+1}\left(\begin{array}{c}2k\\ k\end{array}\right)\left(\begin{array}{c}n\\ 2k\end{array}\right){q}^{n-k},$ where the coefficients form OEIS sequence [21] A055151. In particular, when $q=1$, we have that$|{\mathsf{Pop}}_{{\mathrm{Tam}}_{n}}({\mathrm{Tam}}_{n})|={M}_{n-1},$ where ${M}_{n}$ is the n-th Motzkin number (OEIS sequence [21] A001006).

In the proof of this theorem we also give an exact description of the image of ${\mathsf{Pop}}_{{\mathrm{Tam}}_{n}}$ in terms of 312-avoiding permutations. Additional motivation for studying the size of this image comes from a theorem by Defant and Williams (Theorem 9.13 in [11]). In that theorem, they proved that $|{\mathsf{Pop}}_{{\mathrm{Tam}}_{n}}({\mathrm{Tam}}_{n})|=\{y\in {\mathrm{Tam}}_{n}|\mathsf{Row}(y)\le y\}$, where $\mathsf{Row}$ is the rowmotion operator on ${\mathrm{Tam}}_{n}$ (which is equivalent to the Kreweras complement operator on noncrossing partitions [10]). They also showed that $|{\mathsf{Pop}}_{{\mathrm{Tam}}_{n}}({\mathrm{Tam}}_{n})|$ is the number of independent dominating sets in a certain graph associated with ${\mathrm{Tam}}_{n}$ called its Galois graph.

The paper is organized as follows. In Section 2 we give the necessary definitions. In Section 3 and Section 4 we prove Theorem 1.1 and Theorem 1.2.

## Definition

Assume G is some graph and \gamma is some path of length n on G. In other words, \gamma(1),\dots,\gamma(n) are vertices of G such that \gamma(i) and \gamma(i+1) are connected by an edge. Then the loop erasure of \gamma is a new simple path created by erasing all the loops of \gamma in chronological order. Formally, we define indices i_j inductively using

i_1 = 1\,
i_{j+1}=\max\{k:\gamma(k)=\gamma(i_j)\}+1\,

where "max" here means up to the length of the path \gamma. The induction stops when for some i_j we have \gamma(i_j)=\gamma(n). 

In words, to find i_{j+1}, we hold \gamma(i_j) in one hand, and with the other hand, we trace back from the end: \gamma(n), \gamma(n-1), ..., until we either hit some \gamma(k) = \gamma(i_j) , in which case we set i_{j+1} = k+1, or we end up at \gamma(i_j), in which case we set i_{j+1} = i_j+1.

Assume the induction stops at J i.e. \gamma(i_J)=\gamma(n) is the last i_J. Then the loop erasure of \gamma, denoted by \mathrm{LE}(\gamma) is a simple path of length J defined by

\mathrm{LE}(\gamma)(j)=\gamma(i_j).\,

Now let G be some graph, let v be a vertex of G, and let R be a random walk on G starting from v. Let T be some stopping time for R. Then the loop-erased random walk until time T is LE(R([1,T])). In other words, take R from its beginning until T— that's a (random) path— erase all the loops in chronological order as above— you get a random simple path.

The stopping time T may be fixed, i.e. one may perform n steps and then loop-erase. However, it is usually more natural to take T to be the hitting time in some set. For example, let G be the graph Z^2 and let R be a random walk starting from the point (0,0). Let T be the time when R first hits the circle of radius 100 (we mean here of course a discretized circle). LE(R) is called the loop-erased random walk starting at (0,0) and stopped at the circle.

L30: # The Pop-stack-sorting Operator on Tamari Lattices
L31: 
L32: Letong Hong Address: Department of Mathematics, Massachusetts Institute of Technology, Cambridge, MA 02139 Email address: clhong@mit.edu
L33: 
L34: Date: December 2021
L35: ###### Abstract.
L36: 
L37: Motivated by the pop-stack-sorting map on the symmetric groups, Defant defined an operator $\mathsf{Pop}_{M}:M\to M$ for each complete meet-semilattice $M$ by
L38: 
L39:  | $$\mathsf{Pop}_{M}(x)=\bigwedge(\{y\in M:y\lessdot x\}\cup\{x\}).$$  |
L40: 
L41: This paper concerns the dynamics of $\mathsf{Pop}_{\mathrm{Tam}_{n}}$, where $\mathrm{Tam}_{n}$ is the $n$-th Tamari lattice.
L42: We say an element $x\in\mathrm{Tam}_{n}$ is $t$-$\mathsf{Pop}$-sortable if $\mathsf{Pop}_{M}^{t}(x)$ is the minimal element and we let $h_{t}(n)$ denote the number of $t$-$\mathsf{Pop}$-sortable elements in $\mathrm{Tam}_{n}$. We find an explicit formula for the generating function $\sum_{n\geq 1}h_{t}(n)z^{n}$ and verify Defant’s conjecture that it is rational.
L43: We furthermore prove that the size of the image of $\mathsf{Pop}_{\mathrm{Tam}_{n}}$ is the Motzkin number $M_{n}$, settling a conjecture of Defant and Williams.
L44: ## 1. Introduction
L45: Building on Knuth’s stack-sorting algorithm [cite18†16 ], West’s ground-breaking work on stack-sorting map on symmetric groups [cite19†24 ] inspired subsequent studies, including the reverse-stack-sorting map [cite20†12 ] and the pop-stack-sorting map [cite21†3 ]. Recently, there has been considerable attention by combinatorialists on the pop-stack sorting map [cite22†1 , cite23†2 , cite24†7 , cite25†13 , cite26†20 ].
L46: For each complete meet-semilattice $M$, Defant defined an operator $\mathsf{Pop}_{M}$ that agrees with the pop-stack-sorting map when $M$ is the weak order on $S_{n}$ [cite27†8 ]. It is defined so that $\mathsf{Pop}_{M}$ sends an element to the meet of itself and all elements that it covers. By definition, $M$’s minimal element $\hat{0}$ stays the same when $\mathsf{Pop}_{M}$ is applied. We say an element $x$ is $t$-$\mathsf{Pop}$-sortable if $\mathsf{Pop}_{M}^{t}(x)=\hat{0}$.
L47: Pudwell and Smith [cite26†20 ] enumerated the number of $2$-$\mathsf{Pop}$-sortable elements in $S_{n}$ under the weak order. Claesson and Guðmundsson [cite24†7 ] proved that for each fixed nonnegative integer $t$, the generating function that counts $t$-$\mathsf{Pop}$-sortable elements in $S_{n}$ is rational. Defant [cite28†9 ] established the analogous rationality result for the generating functions of $t$-$\mathsf{Pop}$-sortable elements of type $B$ and type $\widetilde{A}$ weak orders.
L48: Introduced in 1962, the $n$-th Tamari lattice $\mathrm{Tam}_{n}$ consists of semilength-$n$ Dyck paths (lattice paths from $(0,0)$ to $(n,n)$ above the diagonal $y=x$) [cite29†23 ]; its partial order will be defined in Section cite7†2 . There are generalizations of the definition, most notably the $m$-Tamari lattices by Bergeron and Préville-Ratelle [cite30†4 ] and the $\nu$-Tamari lattices introduced by Préville-Ratelle and Viennot [cite31†19 ].
L49: Fundamental in algebraic combinatorics [cite32†17 ], the $n$-th Tamari lattice $\mathrm{Tam}_{n}$ is also isomorphic to $\mathrm{Av}_{n}(312)$, the lattice of $312$-pattern-avoiding permutations under the weak order of $S_{n}$ [cite33†5 ].
L50: In this paper, we study the $\mathsf{Pop}$ operator on Tamari lattices. Let $h_{t}(n)$ be the number of $t$-$\mathsf{Pop}$-sortable elements in $\mathrm{Tam}_{n}$. A part of a conjecture by Defant [cite27†8 ] is that for every fixed $t$, the generating function $\sum_{n\geq 1}h_{t}(n)z^{n}$ is rational. We confirm this statement by giving the exact formula of the generating function:
L51: ###### Theorem 1.1.
L52: 
L53: Let $h_{t}(n)$ denote the number of $t$-$\mathsf{Pop}$-sortable Dyck paths in the $n$-th Tamari lattice $\mathrm{Tam}_{n}$. Then
L54: 
L55:  | $$\sum_{n\geq 1}h_{t}(n)z^{n}=\frac{z}{1-2z-\sum_{j=2}^{t}C_{j-1}z^{j}},$$  |
L56: 
L57: where $C_{j}$ are the Catalan numbers.
L58: 
L59: Moreover, settling a conjecture in Defant and Williams’s paper (Conjecture 11.2 (2) in [cite34†11 ]), we have the following theorem:
L60: ###### Theorem 1.2.
L61: 
L62: Define $\mathsf{Pop}(L;q)=\sum_{b\in\mathsf{Pop}_{L}(L)}q^{|\mathscr{U}_{L}(b)|}$, where $\mathscr{U}_{L}(b)$ is the set of elements of $L$ that cover $b$. Then we have
L63: 
L64:  | $$\mathsf{Pop}(\mathrm{Tam}_{n+1};q)=\sum_{k=0}^{n}\frac{1}{k+1}\binom{2k}{k}\binom{n}{2k}q^{n-k},$$  |
L65: 
L66: where the coefficients form OEIS sequence [cite35†22 ] A055151.
L67: 
L68: In particular, when $q=1$, we have that
L69: 
L70:  | $$|\mathsf{Pop}_{\mathrm{Tam}_{n}}(\mathrm{Tam}_{n})|=M_{n-1},$$  |
L71: where $M_{n}$ is the $n$-th Motzkin number (OEIS sequence [cite35†22 ] A001006).
L72: Additional motivation for studying the size of the image of $\mathsf{Pop}_{\mathrm{Tam}_{n}}$ comes from a theorem by Defant and Williams (Theorem 9.13 in [cite34†11 ]). In that theorem, they proved that $|X_{n}|=\{y\in\mathrm{Tam}_{n}\mid\mathsf{Row}(y)\leq y\}$, where $\mathsf{Row}$ is the rowmotion operator on $\mathrm{Tam}_{n}$ (which is equivalent to the Kreweras complement operator on noncrossing partitions [cite36†10 ]).
L73: They also showed that $|X_{n}|$ is the number of independent dominating sets in a certain graph associated with $\mathrm{Tam}_{n}$ called its Galois graph.
L74: The paper is organized as follows. In Section cite7†2 we give the necessary definitions. In Section cite10†3 and Section cite13†4 we prove cite37†Theorem 1.1 and cite38†Theorem 1.2 .

L80: ### 2.1. Lattice basics and the $\mathsf{Pop}$ operator.
L81: ###### Definition 2.1.
L82: A meet-semilattice is a poset $M$ such that any two elements $x,y\in M$ have a greatest lower bound (which is called their meet, denoted by $x\wedge y$). A lattice $L$ is a meet-semilattice such that any two elements $x,y\in L$ also have a least upper bound (which is called their join, denoted by $x\vee y$). A meet-semilattice is complete if every nonempty subset $A\subset M$ has a meet.
L83: Given $x,y\in M$, we say that $y$ is covered by $x$ (denoted $y\lessdot x$) if $y<x$ and no $z\in M$ satisfies $y<z<x$.
L84: In this paper we only consider finite meet-semilattices, each of which has a unique minimal element $\hat{0}$. They are automatically complete.
L85: ###### Definition 2.2 ([cite27†8 ]).
L86: 
L87: Let $M$ be a complete meet-semilattice. Define the semilattice pop-stack-sorting operator $\mathsf{Pop}_{M}:M\to M$ by
L88: 
L89:  | $$\mathsf{Pop}_{M}(x)=\bigwedge(\{y\in M:y\lessdot x\}\cup\{x\}).$$  |
L90: 
L91: ###### Definition 2.3.
L92: 
L93: We say an element $x$ of a complete meet-semilattice $M$ is $t$-$\mathsf{Pop}$-sortable if $\mathsf{Pop}^{t}(x)=\hat{0}$.
L94: ### 2.2. Generalized Tamari lattices.
L95: 
L96: In this paper, a lattice path is a finite planar path that starts from the origin and at each step travels either up/$\rm{N}:(0,1)$ or right/$\rm{E}:(1,0)$.

L100: The horizontal distance of a point $p$ with respect to a lattice path $\nu$ is the maximum number of east steps one can take starting from $p$ before being strictly to the right of $\nu$.

L103: Let $\nu$ be a lattice path from $(0,0)$ to $(\ell-n,n)$. The generalized $\nu$- Tamari lattice $\mathrm{Tam}(\nu)$ is defined as follows:

L121: ### 3.1. Preliminaries: the $\nu$-bracket vector.
L122: ###### Definition 3.1.
L123: 
L124: Let $\mathbf{b}(\nu)=(b_{0}(\nu),b_{1}(\nu),\ldots,b_{\ell}(\nu))$ be the vector denoting the heights at each step of the lattice path $\nu$. Let the fixed position $f_{k}$ denote the largest index such that $b_{f_{k}}(\nu)=k$. We say that an integer vector $\vec{\mathsf{b}}=(\mathsf{b}_{0},\mathsf{b}_{1},\ldots,\mathsf{b}_{\ell})$ is a $\nu$-bracket vector, denoted as $\vec{\mathsf{b}}\in\rm{Vec}(\nu)$, if
L125: 
L126:   1. (1)
L127: 
L128: $\mathsf{b}_{f_{k}}=k$ for all $k=0,\ldots,n$.
L129: 
L130:   2. (2)
L131: $b_{i}(\nu)\leq\mathsf{b}_{i}\leq n$ for all $0\leq i\leq\ell$.
L132: 
L133:   3. (3)
L134: 
L135: If $\mathsf{b}_{i}=k$, then $\mathsf{b}_{j}\leq k$ for all $i+1\leq j\leq f_{k}$.
L136: 
L137: The partial order of $\rm{Vec}(\nu)$ is defined as follows: we say $(\mathsf{b}_{0},\mathsf{b}_{1},\ldots,\mathsf{b}_{\ell})\leq(\mathsf{b}^{\prime}_{0},\mathsf{b}^{\prime}_{1},\ldots,\mathsf{b}^{\prime}_{\ell})$ if $\mathsf{b}_{i}\leq\mathsf{b}^{\prime}_{i}$ for all $i$.

L140: An equivalent interpretation of (3) is that $\vec{\mathsf{b}}$ is 121-pattern-avoiding. These conditions also imply the sequence $\{\mathsf{b}_{i}\}_{f_{k-1}+1}^{f_{k}}$ is non-increasing for all $k=0,\ldots,n$.

L34: # Scaling limits of loop-erased Markov chains on resistance spaces via a partial loop-erasing procedure
L35: 
L36: Shiping Cao Address: Department of Mathematics, University of Washington, Seattle 98105, USA Email address: spcao@uw.edu
L37: ###### Abstract.
L38: We introduce partial loop-erasing operators. We show that by applying a refinement sequence of partial loop-erasing operators to a finite Markov chain, we get a process equivalent to the chronological loop-erased Markov chain. As an application, we construct loop-erased random paths on bounded domains of resistance spaces as the weak limit of the loop erasure of the Markov chains on a sequence of finite sets approximating the space, and the limit is independent of the approximating sequences.
L39: The random paths we constructed are simple paths almost surely, and they can be viewed as the loop-erasure of the paths of the diffusion process. Finally, we show that the scaling limit of the loop-erased random walks on the Sierpiński carpet graphs exists, and is equivalent to the loop-erased random paths on the Sierpińksi carpet.

L47: ## 1. introduction
L48: 
L49: In the 1980’s, Lawler introduced loop-erased random walks (LERW) in [cite22†35 ], and the model later gains much interest due to its connection with uniform spanning trees [cite23†46 , cite24†49 , cite25†55 ].
L50: One of the natural questions about LERWs is the existence of their scaling limits. On Euclidean spaces, significant progress has been made over the past few decades. First, as a main result of [cite22†35 ], Lawler showed that, in the high dimensional cases ($d\geq 5$), the scaling limit of LERW on $\mathbb{Z}^{d}$ exists and is the same as the Brownian motion on $\mathbb{R}^{d}$. A similar result holds in the $d=4$ case [cite26†36 , cite27†37 , cite28†38 ] with an additional logarithmic correction in time.
L51: The question becomes more delicate for $d=2,3$ cases. On $\mathbb{R}^{2}$, Lawler, Schramm and Werner [cite29†41 ] proved that the scaling limit exists, which is characterized by SLE_{2} [cite30†52 ]. On $\mathbb{R}^{3}$, Kozma proved the existence of the scaling limit [cite31†32 ]. It was shown later in [cite32†50 ] by Sapozhnikov and Shiraishi that the limit is almost surely a simple path.
L52: Moreover, a time parameterized scaling limit is obtained recently in [cite33†42 ] on $\mathbb{R}^{2}$, and in [cite34†43 ] on $\mathbb{R}^{3}$. The reader is referred to [cite35†26 , cite36†47 , cite37†51 ] for the study of the growth rate of LERW.
L53: In this paper, we focus on establishing the existence of the scaling limit of LERW on some fractal spaces. In fact, in earlier works [cite38†21 , cite39†22 ], K. Hattori and M. Mizuno have studied LERW on Sierpiński gasket graphs, using an ‘erasing-larger-loops-first’ algorithm. Inspired by their idea, in this paper, we will develop a much simpler and more general algorithm. Using the new algorithm, we can naturally define loop-erased random paths (LERP) on a large class of spaces, including many fractals.
L54: More precisely, in a proper local resistance space [cite40†29 , cite41†30 , cite42†31 ], we will define LERP as the weak limit in Hausdorff metric of the loop erasure of Markov chains on finite sets approximating the domain.
L55: Typical examples of resistance spaces are strongly local regular Dirichlet spaces that have sub-Gaussian heat kernel estimates with the walk dimension [cite43†1 , cite44†8 , cite45†17 ] greater than the Hausdorff dimension (as a consequence of the Sobolev embedding theorem, see Theorem 4.11 of [cite45†17 ] for example).
L56: The author hopes that these results can be extended to more general settings in the future, in particular, dropping the condition about the pointwise recurrence: every point has positive capacity in a resistance space.

On the other hand, the PLE operator associated with $\widetilde{V}\subset V$ is that we only erase loops about points in $\widetilde{V}$.
